hard_spots.why_hard: Potato is hard, gritty/crunchy (ざくざく), as if frozen, tasteless/nasty (不味). Period poor-cooking/storage detail. Keep physical and uninterpreted; do not make it symbolize poverty or turn causality explicit (potato = vision). English must keep teeth, coldness, lack of taste without ennobling or explaining.

幻のような絵, 淡暗い光り, 物静か — picture stays a picture seen by the eye, not a dream entered or doctrine concluded. Do not translate 絵 as vision/scene/world, 幻 as hallucination/dream, or upgrade dimness into mysticism.

懐かしみ (natsukashimi), 許し, 安らかさ, 安息 — repeated network. Natsukashimi is fond remembrance/longing, not nostalgia in modern English sense and not forgiveness; 許し is pardon/forgiveness. Keep same English words each time; do not expand into explanations or merge them.

あの日, 永久に夜のような安息 — that day / night-like rest. Could imply death, old age, eternity, judgement. Text leaves open. Keep literal 'that day' and 'rest like night'; do not name heaven, death, afterlife, or judgement day.

Child explicitly girl but called 坊や (Bōya, literally boy). Period affectionate generic for baby. Keep 'Bōya' (romanised, explained in margin once) rather than 'boy/son/little one' which either misgenders or erases the wrinkle, and do not invent a name.

卓《テーブル》, 土瓶, アルミ鍋, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》 — Taishō literary with old kana and ruby glosses. Table is Western-style table under bare bulb; aluminium pot, earthen teapot, beef/onion/carrot/potato mark pauvre modernity. Render plainly without exoticizing or modernizing; ruby shows reading, not emphasis.

motifs.english: Keep one short word: 'storm'. Same noun in p1 announcement, p8 unheard, p19 heard alone, p38 whisper. Do not vary to tempest/gale or swell last line into symbol.
motifs.why: Acoustic frame that opens, disappears, and closes the story. Its return marks contraction back to present.

motifs.english: Keep 'smile' for 微笑/ほほえみ/笑み/笑い throughout, even where English would vary to grin/laugh. Child's noise vs parents' helpless smiling is the first-movement music.
motifs.why: Deliberate chain linking domestic laughter to the still smiling of the three figures; varying breaks the link.

motifs.english: Keep 'eyes / gaze' stable. 瞳 for soft deep looking, 眼 for lifted/strained looking. Do not upgrade to stare/gaze shifting.
motifs.why: Attention is the story's action: parents gaze at child, mother gazes far, vision is seen in eye's bottom.

motifs.english: Keep 'far / far off / far heart' literally, even repetitively. Distance becomes a place, not a metaphor to tidy.
motifs.why: Ordinary diction of distance carries the slide out of time; paraphrase would rationalize it.

motifs.english: Keep 'all / everything' for すべて/総て. Flat and total, not 'whole world' or 'life'.
motifs.why: Totalizing word that lets vision claim everything (good/evil/sorrow/joy) without showing any event.

motifs.english: Keep 'long' for ながい/永く. Do not vary to endless/eternal except where Japanese says 絶えることなく/永久に.
motifs.why: Three years feel long; story told is long; suffering after is long. Repetition makes 'only three years' land.

motifs.english: Keep 'quiet/still/silent' family together: 静か, 黙って, 黙る, 静まりかへった. Silence set against noise and against husband's 'why are you silent?'
motifs.why: Second half is defined by mother's silence against first-half racket; husband's repeated question marks it.

motifs.english: Keep 'tiredness / weary' for 疲れ/だるそう/打沈んだ. Physical, shared, young yet exhausted; do not pathologize.
motifs.why: Establishes poverty of strength without wrinkles; motivates but does not explain vision.

motifs.english: Keep fixed trio: 'fond remembrance (natsukashimi) and forgiveness and peace'. Gloss natsukashimi once in margin; thereafter same words. 'That day' stays 'that day'.
motifs.motif: fond remembrance, forgiveness, peace / night-like rest
motifs.why: Vision's whole content is these nouns; any elegant variation turns summary into doctrine.

motifs.english: Keep wife's exact refrain 'only three years / barely three years' (p14, p22, p27) and husband's echo 'only two years past' (p25, p28). Do not improve her inarticulacy.
motifs.motif: only three years; just a little longer; let's work
motifs.why: Contraction back to ordinary time and unexalted endurance; mother's eloquence must stay limited to this.

narration.english_tense: Simple past throughout as default. Keep explanatory past (it was, it was that) for p2-p4 scene-setting and for gnomic vision summary p17; do not switch vision to present timeless or dialogue to present.
narration.frame: One supper in a small room under a dark bulb, storm outside. Narration begins external and comic-crowded, drifts with mother without scene-break, contracts to table-clearing and whispered storm.
narration.narrator: Third-person external narrator, initially distanced (親子, 男, 女), imperceptibly becoming mother's interior focalization from p10-p11 onward. No italics, no dream-marking, no psychologizing verbs; hedges (いつか, ふと, いつとなく, なにか, ように) and explanatory endings (であった, のであった, のだった) keep reverie in same grammar as table.
narration.tense_habits: Japanese past/explanatory (であった, のであった, のだった) for both outer fact and inner summary; progressive/distal forms (〜しつつ, 〜ようとしてゐる, 〜てゐた) for ongoing supper vs completed drift. Hedged perception verbs, not marked thought.
timeline: p1-p9: crowded comic supper — baby stands holding table, bangs spoon, parents sweep everything below table, forget storm in racket
p10-p11: trigger — mother serves beef/onion/carrot/potato from blue pot, tastes hard gritty tasteless potato, falls vaguely silent
p12-p18: expansion — three married years feel lifelong, sufferings recalled dreamlike, phantom-like picture of three telling endless story, night-like rest ahead
p19-p32: return punctured by dialogue — husband twice 'why are you silent?', wife can only say 'only three years', husband answers 'two years past, baby will walk, a little longer', feeding resumes
p33-p38: close — chopsticks laid down, nursing, clear table sleep early tomorrow, child asleep at breast, stillness, husband stands whispering storm

style_sheet.annotation_density: Sparse; margin only where sentence cannot give reader the thing: Bōya (affectionate address for baby despite girl child), aluminium pot / beef-pot supper as poverty-modernity, 懐かしみ gloss once, old-kana ruby convention. Never annotate what context supplies or explain that day.
style_sheet.author_voice: Taishō literary but not quaint: soft, slightly formal, accumulative long sentences with repetitions, then short dialogue punctures. Keep drift in same diction as table; no italics for thought, no vividness upgrade for vision, no sentimentality for baby, no consolation conclusion. Husband's practical hope stands equal to vision.
style_sheet.honorifics_and_names: No personal names in text. Use 'the man / the young father', 'the woman / the mother', 'the child / the baby' as Japanese does; do not normalize to husband/wife/father/mother throughout. Keep 'Bōya' for 坊や as address with one margin note; do not translate to boy/son/baby.
style_sheet.keep_in_japanese: Bōya only, in romanisation with macron-less plain form. All else in English: Sensei-type retention does not apply (no 先生). Foods, vessels (rice, aluminium pot, earthen teapot, tea-bowl) in plain English.
style_sheet.quotation: Japanese 『』 for direct speech and ひとりで独言. In English use double quotation marks for spoken lines (p7, p21-p35, p38 whisper). Husband's どうして黙ってるの twice must read as same question. Do not join dialogue to narration or split drift sentences to make logic clearer.
style_sheet.register: Clean, soft, slightly formal past-tense English. Poverty plain without ennoblement; comedy bodily without cuteness; abstraction flat without elegance. Repeat words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese varies. The mother's spoken lines are kept short and unsoftened, so her coldness is in their brevity.
style_sheet.ruby_and_italics: Ruby in source (卓《テーブル》, 怜悧《れいり》, 微笑《ほほゑみ》) shows reading; render as normal English ('table', 'shrewd', 'smile') with no italics. No italics for vision or thought. Italics only for Bōya as foreign address on first use if house style requires, then roman.

Style sheet, register: added that the mother's spoken lines are kept short and unsoftened, so her coldness is in their brevity.
Reading, voice take 'Quiet drift (recommended)': the mother is now cold and halting, her short lines left unsoftened.

crux.for_the_english: So: keep the trigger physical and uninterpreted. The potato is hard — “as if frozen”, gritty between her teeth, tasteless — and the distance it opens in her is rendered in the narration's ordinary diction of distance itself (“far”, “far off”, “far heart”, “rate”, repeated until it becomes a place). Do not name what she sees: not heaven, not death, not her own old age, not a judgement day, though it has something of all of them. “あの日” is only “that day”. The picture must stay a picture — 幻のような絵, “a picture like a phantom”, something her eye sees, not a doctrine she arrives at. An English version that upgrades the vision into consolation — that lets her (or the narrator) conclude anything — has written a religious tract over a story about a bad potato. Likewise keep the return unexalted: “もう少しの間だ” — “just a little longer” — nursing the child, clearing the table, getting up early tomorrow. The vision does not solve the poverty. It sits next to it, and the story ends not on it but on a man standing still, whispering, 「嵐だな」 — “a storm”. That bare last line is the frame closing: the storm announced in p1, unheard through the child's noise in p8, heard by her alone inside her silence in p19, and finally heard by everyone in the quiet of p37–38. Keep it exactly that plain and that short; do not let it swell into a symbol at the last moment.
crux.point: "The crux is the mother's mid-mouthful slide out of time. For five paragraphs this is a warm, crowded, slightly comic supper: a fat baby girl just able to stand by holding the table, banging a spoon, everything swept out of her reach, two young parents — not a wrinkle on either face, but a deep, drowsy tiredness already in his hollowed eyes and her fine shoulders — laughing helplessly and forgetting, in the racket, even to hear the storm outside. Then, in p10–p11, the mother puts a potato in her mouth. It is hard, gritty, as if frozen, thoroughly nasty. She says nothing. And the prose, without any marker of a scene-change, drifts with her: the three years since her marriage stretch until she feels she has lived a whole long life and grown quite old; the sufferings of those three years come back “dreamlike”, and she is suddenly seeing, from very far away, a dim picture (絵) of three people with their heads together telling one endless story in which everything — good and evil, sorrow, suffering, anger, joy — is told, while nobody moves, nobody is disturbed, and all of it is wrapped in 懐かしみ (natsukashimi, fond remembrance) and 許し (forgiveness) and a deep peace like the night's. The story stands or falls on whether the English lets that expansion happen inside an ordinary sentence at an ordinary table, and then lets it contract again to “only three years” (p14, p22, p27) and to work tomorrow."
crux.why: Everything else in the text serves that one movement. The frame is built for it: storm heard / storm unheard / storm heard again. The child's noise in the first movement is not decoration — it is what the world sounds like from inside a life being lived at full stretch, and the mother's silence in the second half is set against her husband's repeated, puzzled 「どうして黙ってるの」 (“why are you so quiet?”, p19, p21) precisely because he cannot follow her where she has gone. And the vision's content is all summary and no event: nothing is shown happening, only everything having already happened and turned, in the telling, into fondness and pardon. If the English makes the vision vivid, specific or dramatic, the ratio inverts and it becomes a fantasy interrupting a domestic sketch, rather than the domestic sketch briefly seen from the far side of a whole life.

open_questions.question: Who are the three people in dim picture? Family aged, themselves in afterlife, humanity generic? Text keeps three quiet people, heads together. Don't identify.
open_questions.why_it_matters: If identified as family in old age/heaven, vision becomes specific consolation and loses universality/ambiguity.

open_questions.question: "That day" when all becomes nostalgia/forgiveness - death, old age, far future, eternity before night-like rest? Keep literal that day/night-like rest unresolved.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Naming death/heaven clarifies author's deliberate vagueness and changes theology/tone.

open_questions.question: Baby explicitly girl in p2, yet parents call her Bōya (boy/baby lad). Keep Bōya as affectionate generic 'baby/little one' without correcting gender or inventing name?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Correcting to 'little girl' erases period colloquial address; transliterating unexplained confuses.

open_questions.question: Potato: frozen-like hard gritty undercooked potato - literal poor cooking/storage period detail, not metaphor invented. Keep texture words close.
open_questions.why_it_matters: Symbolising potato destroys crux trigger's ordinariness.

reading.reading: The crux must stay first in drafting. Beyond it, notice the narration's slide: begins outside ('a parent and child', 'the man', 'the woman') and imperceptibly becomes the mother's interior in same past-tense explanatory endings (de atta / no datta) and same 'as if', 'somehow', 'before she knew it' hedges. No italics, dreams marked, or psychologising verbs should separate reverie. Long sentences accumulate repetitions - smile (hohoemi), eyes/gaze, quiet/still, dream, all/everything (subete), long (nagai), far - then dialogue punctures with short exchanges. Repeat English words even unfashionably; vary only when Japanese does. Register Taishō literary with old kana but not quaint: clean, soft, slightly formal English, poverty plain (rice, aluminium pot, beef onion carrot potato) without ennobling supper. Parents unnamed, young yet exhausted; child noisy bodily comedy prevents sentimentality. Husband's practical hope ('little one will soon walk', 'let's work') not lesser than vision. Fluent risks: rationalising potato-to-vision causality, clarifying 'that day', expanding abstract nouns into explanations, destroying rhythm by splitting drift or joining dialogue, impoverishing subete/nagai/far repetitions, making mother eloquent - she can say almost nothing, repeatedly 'only three years', and husband misunderstands kindly.

voice_takes.label: Quiet drift (recommended)
voice_takes.line: "叙述は温かい同室の声から、区切りなく母の遠い心へ滑る" — narration slides without break from warm room to mother's far heart. Clean slightly formal prose, long looping sentences, repeated plain words; parents young plainspoken, husband blunt warm ('sa da naa' as soft 'that's so'), mother cold and halting, her short lines left unsoftened; wrong: lyrical uplift, heaven language, modern therapy idiom, cute baby-talk.

voice_takes.label: Plainer and drier
voice_takes.line: Shorter English sentences, abstract nouns kept bare (fondness, forgiveness, peace) without softening, dialogue working-plain. Risk: vision reads stark/fatalistic rather than tender.

voice_takes.label: Slightly period-formal
voice_takes.line: More formal diction and slower cadence matching 1917 literary surface, parents courteous-distanced. Risk: archaism makes poverty picturesque and mother remote, wrong if it sounds translated-old rather than young.

data.reply: I've taken you to mean her spoken lines only: they are now shorter and colder in her cast entry and the style sheet, and in the 'Quiet drift' take she is cold and halting with her lines left unsoftened. I haven't touched the narration, the husband or the child, because her coldness belongs in what she says at the table, not in the voice that drifts with her; that drift, and the crux it serves, are unchanged.
data.say: The mother's dialogue was made shorter and colder, unsoftened, in her cast entry, the style sheet and the recommended voice take, with the narration and crux left unchanged.
